articles.title: Jennifer Aniston Is Focused on This 1 Aspect of Healthy Aging — and Weight Lifting Is Helping Her Get There
articles.summary: Jennifer Aniston can sum up her old workout routine in three words: “cardio, cardio, cardio.”
articles.body: Jennifer Aniston can sum up her old workout routine in three words: “cardio, cardio, cardio.” “Treadmill, elliptical, bike. Treadmill, elliptical, bike,” she says. “Rinse and repeat.” Weights were always part of it, but her routine primarily tacked on just five to 10 minutes of lifting to the end of a workout, and usually only five to eight pounds dumbbells. It was all a reflection of the “messaging” at the time, she says, that weights will make you bulky. “You hear bulk, and you kind of run for the hills if you’re a woman, a young girl,” she says. “You want to be lean, lean, lean. And the thought of bulk and weight makes you go, ‘It’ll get big, big, big,’ and you just go, ‘No, no, no.’” Now, speaking to TODAY.com about her new 30-day strength training program with boutique fitness studio Pvolve, she says, “if only I’d listened” to those calls for people, women especially, to preserve their bone density through weight lifting. She’s not alone. Pvolve released a movement longevity report that found that 78% of respondents (1,000 women over age 40) to an online survey know weight lifting is important. But 60% don’t do it in a typical week. The reasons range from not knowing where to start (27%), fears of injury (20%) and feeling intimidated by weights (9%), per the report. Aniston, 57, says she really started to implement strength training into her routine through Pvolve. She started using the fitness method, which offers at-home, on demand workouts, in 2021 as a “secret streamer” after an injury, before joining Pvolve as a public partner in 2023. She says she also got injured after trying boxing and CrossFit. “To each their own, but I just would find myself injured quite a lot,” she says. “And granted, I’m a little klutzy.” “But Pvolve has just sort of changed all that,” she adds. It’s also changed her understanding of what defines a successful workout. She says when her routine was entirely cardio-focused, if she wasn’t drenched in sweat and “heaving” by the end, it didn’t feel like progress. Once she started incorporating weights in her entire workouts, she prioritized consistency, gradual weight increases and listening to her body. “You feel sore, but it’s never sore to the point where you can’t walk the next day ... well, sometimes, but in a good way,” she says. “I’ve had workouts where I really can’t walk or walking up a step or two or having to sit down was just agony. That feels like you worked something too hard.” Aniston’s strength training approach is to add weights to the “everyday” movements she already did with Pvolve. The moves are often compound, meaning they work multiple muscle groups at a time, and require balance. Her workouts get at the “little tiny micro muscles that are hiding underneath the big muscles,” she says. Weight lifting is also known to protect bone density, or how porous bones are, which deteriorates with age. Dr. Ian Smith told TODAY.com the best time to build up bone density is in your 20s, when bone mass is at its peak. That way, you have more you can stand to lose as you age. But you can still preserve what remains and slow future loss at any age through weight-bearing exercises, which puts muscle and bone under strain to promote growth. “I wish we had listened to this when we were told, but we didn’t. ... Bone density is something we talk about now a lot,” Aniston says. “My parents were lucky enough to live quite long in life, but they were not mobile,” she adds. “This is all about longevity, and growing old is in all of our cards, so how do we do that with as much strength and mobility so we can thrive?” For Aniston, she takes it workout by workout. “Consistency is everything, and then you just feel stronger and you realize, you know what, I can go up to a 10-pounder,’” she says. But listening to her body is paramount, she says. “Give yourself a day off if you don’t want to work out ... Don’t dread it,” she says. “Just check in and just say, you know what, I’ll start, and if I don’t feel great after five minutes, and I still feel like s---, then I just don’t work out.” “Or, I just go, ‘You know how great you’re going to feel when you’re done?’ You’re going to feel so amazing,” she says. “You can do anything for 40 minutes, come on.”

articles.body: Star Meat Delivery Inc. of Lucama, North Carolina, is recalling approximately 167,639 pounds of raw pork, beef and goat products, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture announcement posted Tuesday. The items were produced without the benefit of federal inspection, meaning they weren’t confirmed to be “safe, wholesome and properly labeled” by the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS). The recalled meat is also labeled with a false USDA mark of inspection, the announcement added. This recall has been classified as class I, the highest health risk. This classification refers to “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death,” according to the U.S. Food & Drug Administration. Which Products Are Being Recalled? Any meat product produced by Star Meat Delivery Inc. with an inspection and establishment number that reads “EST. 1363” is falsely labeled, according to the announcement. Consider it misbranded and unsafe to eat, the FSIS warned. The vacuum-sealed raw pork, beef and goat products were produced on various dates before Sept. 22, 2026. They were packed into cardboard boxes ahead of shipping, and once they arrived at their destinations, may have been relabeled with the respective retailer’s sticker and handling instructions, the announcement said. articles.title: Israel’s ambassador to the US says son injured in West Bank car-ramming
articles.summary: Palestinian shot dead as Israel’s ambassador to the US identifies injured soldier as his son.
articles.body:
Israel’s Ambassador to the United States Yechiel Leiter has said his son, a soldier, was injured in an alleged car-ramming incident west of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

Earlier on Wednesday, a Palestinian man was shot dead by Israeli forces following what Israeli police described as a car-ramming attack that injured a soldier at a checkpoint at an intersection near the illegal Israeli settlement of Beit Horon, Israeli police said in a brief statement.

Leiter said in a social media post that medics “are now fighting to save the life of Neria Dov ben Chana”, referring to his son.

Later, Shaare Zedek Hospital said the soldier underwent a complex surgery, and his life remains at risk.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the wounded soldier in hospital before departing for the United States to his planned address to the United Nations General Assembly, according to his office.

In a post on X, Netanyahu wrote, “I recently visited the dear family of Neria Leiter…I ask you to pray for the recovery of Neria Dov ben Chana. The entire nation is with you”.

In an earlier post Netanyahu wrote, “My wife Sara and I, together with all the people of Israel, are praying for a miracle”.

Another son of Leiter’s, 39-year-old Moshe Yedidya, was killed while deployed in Gaza in November 2023, just weeks after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave on October 7.

Meanwhile, the Palestinian Health Ministry identified the suspected attacker as 29-year-old Mahmoud Mohammad Mahmoud Suleiman, adding that Israeli authorities were holding his body.

Beit Ur al-Tahta Mayor Hazem Suleiman, who is not related to Mahmoud Suleiman, was quoted by the AFP news agency as saying that Israeli forces raided the village and searched the man’s family home.

“The town is closed off, with all its entrances blocked. There is no social or commercial activity and no signs of normal life,” he said, adding that the army had also searched other houses.

articles.title: Accident victim taken to 2 Ghaziabad hospitals: Turned away by 1, other too costly; dies
articles.summary: 24-year-old Ghaziabad accident victim died after treatment delays at two hospitals; family alleges fee demands despite PM-RAHAT cashless care scheme.
articles.body: GHAZIABAD: A 24-year-old man seriously injured in a bike accident died after a long delay in treatment despite reaching two hospitals, one of which allegedly didn’t have the right doctor present while the other, according to his father, was more concerned about payments than giving him the medical attention he urgently needed to survive.Tushar Kumar’s ordeal flies in the face of Supreme Court’s scathing observations in a recent case where a minor rape survivor was turned away by two Ghaziabad hospitals and died on the way to a third.The court also said it would frame national guidelines so that hospitals cannot show negligence in treating victims of serious crimes and those requiring immediate medical attention.Besides, Prime Minister-Road Accident Victims’ Hospitalisation and Assured Treatment (PM-RAHAT) scheme, notified by the road transport ministry, guarantees cashless treatment of up to Rs 1.5 lakh per person to accident victims at empanelled hospitals. Atlanta Hospital, where Kumar was first taken, is an empanelled one.A resident of Prahaladgarhi in Vashundhara, Kumar was hit by a vehicle on Link Road, about 100 metres from Namo Bharat Sahibabad station around 2.30am while he was on his way home from a hotel where he worked as a waiter. Cops were alerted by passersby on Dial 112.Police said they took the injured biker to Atlanta in Vasundhara, about 2 km away, which referred him to another hospital. He was subsequently taken to Yashoda Medicity in Indirapuram 5km away.Tushar’s father Shiv told TOI that Yashoda Medicity asked him to submit part of the admission fees. “As the charges were high, we thought of shifting him to a govt hospital and requested the hospital to arrange an ambulance, for which they asked me to pay Rs 6,000 upfront. When I returned with money, they asked me to pay another Rs 48,000 for the treatment administered to Tushar,” Shiv, who is a daily wage worker, said. He claimed the hospital refused to release Tushar till the family cleared the bill.“I arranged the funds from some moneylenders and cleared the bill, but I still don’t know why they charged Rs 48,000 when they did not provide any treatment to my son,” he said.Tushar, his father claimed, had reached Yashoda Medicity around 3 am, and it was 8 am when he was finally discharged and taken to Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi, 26 km away, where he died during treatment around 4am on Sept 20.“Atlanta and Yashoda both played a role in my son’s death. One hospital refused to treat him, and the other delayed his release and also delayed his treatment by that extent just to earn money,” he said.Atlanta Hospital COO Dr Mahesh Chaudhary told TOI that initial treatment was given after Tushar was brought to the hospital by police. “But Tushar’s condition was critical as his hands and legs were severed in the accident and he needed a vascular surgeon at the time. We did not have the facilities to treat him properly, and that is why we advised the police to take him to a bigger hospital for treatment,” Chaudhary said.A statement from the Yashoda Medicity administration said following admission, Tushar was assessed by the medical team and appropriate treatment was initiated based on his clinical condition, with priority given to providing life-saving medical care. “Throughout the period of treatment, the hospital made every reasonable effort to support the patient’s clinical needs and also extended a concession during the interim period. Following clinical assessment and the treatment provided, the patient and family were counselled regarding the further course of care and advised accordingly,” it said.According to police, while Atlanta is empanelled under the PM-RAHAT scheme, Yashoda is not. Indirapuram ACP Suryabali Maurya said police took Tushar to Yashoda Medicity, even though it was not empanelled under the central govt scheme, to save his life within the ‘golden hour’ on the suggestion of doctors at Atlanta. “An FIR was filed against an unknown vehicle driver under BNS sections 106 (death due to negligence) and 281 (rash driving) at Indirapuram police station. Teams have been formed to scan CCTV footage and nab the accused,” the ACP said.Health department officials said information on empanelled hospitals, including their names and locations, has been shared with police officials at different levels, including police stations and senior officers, as well as emergency service providers. “The objective is to ensure that once an accident is reported, the responding personnel can quickly identify the nearest PM-RAHAT-designated hospital and arrange for the victim to be shifted there without losing critical time,” said health department nodal officer (road safety) Dr Pankaj Rakesh.(With inputs from Ayantika Pal)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: What is kratom? Risks of popular substance revealed after college students' deaths
articles.summary: Two University of Mississippi students died with kratom found at both scenes, raising urgent questions about the substance's opioid-like effects.
articles.body: The deaths of two University of Mississippi students have raised fresh questions about the potential health risks of kratom. The students died Monday at separate locations on campus. During both investigations, authorities recovered packaged kratom that was purchased from a retail store, according to a Lafayette County Metro Narcotics news release shared by the Oxford Police Department. Authorities have not confirmed whether the substance played a role in the students’ deaths. PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH SPARKS QUESTIONS ABOUT OVERDOSE, WITHDRAWAL AND REHAB SAFETY Kratom is a plant-based substance often marketed as a natural option for pain relief or opioid withdrawal, but experts warn that it can cause dependence, dangerous interactions and other serious health complications. "Kratom acts as a stimulant at low doses, which could provoke heart arrhythmia," Fox News senior medical analyst, Dr. Marc Siegel told Fox News Digital. "At high doses, it acts more like an opioid, and so can suppress breathing." Kratom is widely available, Jessica Steinman, chief clinical officer at No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, told Fox News Digital. "We are starting to see it in storefronts, at your local gas stations, smoke shops and health food stores, where it's being sold as an energy booster," she said. "People are starting to buy it over the counter and use it incorrectly, and use mass amounts of it." DR DREW PINSKY REVEALS RED FLAG IN PRESLEY GERBER ADDICTION TREATMENT BEFORE MODEL'S DEATH "It's affecting the opioid receptors in people's brains," she went on. "It can cause them to be overly sedated, it can slow down their breathing and general function of their lungs." Kratom can also become highly addictive, Steinman warned. Traditional kratom products generally contain lower levels of active compounds, while newer 7-OH products are often concentrated or enhanced to produce stronger, more stimulating effects, she noted. 7-OH products contain 7-hydroxymitragynine, a potent opioid-related compound found in kratom. AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING Although kratom laws vary by state and locality, Steinman said regulators are increasingly focused on the concentrated 7-OH products and synthetic kratom-related compounds, rather than traditional botanical kratom containing only trace amounts of 7-OH. As to why there has been an uptick in kratom use among young people, Steinman said she believes many of them are learning about it from social media or through their friends. "People are starting to buy it over the counter and use it incorrectly, and use mass amounts of it." College students may be using the substance for two reasons, she said. "One reason would be, it is a stimulant," Steinman noted. "They may have pressures to stay awake, to study, get good grades … they may want to be more energized." People may also be using it due to its opioid-like effects, the expert said. "It does give someone that sedating high, that kind of numbing out from feeling anything very difficult, not wanting to have to deal with stress or anxiety." It becomes more dangerous when people combine it with multiple substances, like alcohol, marijuana or benzodiazepines. "That's when it can become lethal," Steinman warned. When to seek medical attention People who use kratom and begin breathing slowly or shallowly, or who become excessively drowsy or difficult to awaken, may be experiencing serious sedation that can interfere with breathing, Steinman said. In those cases, prompt medical care is important. "Another issue that isn't really talked about often is when people might possibly get addicted to kratom," she cautioned. SORORITY RUSH GETS OZEMPIC MAKEOVER AS SOME COLLEGE WOMEN RESORT TO WEIGHT-LOSS INJECTIONS Reducing or abruptly stopping kratom after regular use can trigger withdrawal, and in some cases may lead to seizures, according to the expert. Anyone experiencing a seizure should seek emergency medical care. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Steinman also responded to those who might claim that kratom is safe due to the fact that it’s a natural substance. "Just because something's from the earth doesn't make it healthy — people can get addicted and compulsive with lots of things," she said. The expert pointed out that there are no addictive components to marijuana, but it becomes addictive – "not necessarily addictive to the brain, but to the feeling that it gives you." "And that's the same situation with kratom – people get addicted to that feeling. But with kratom, it's actually affecting the opioid receptors in the brain." Industry response Dallas Vasquez, CEO and co-founder of Mitra9 Brands, a Florida-based company that manufactures and sells beverages and products containing kratom (mitragynine) and kava, emphasized the difference between botanical kratom products containing trace levels of 7-OH and products formulated with added, enhanced, highly concentrated or synthesized 7-OH. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The FDA has specifically identified added or enhanced 7-OH products as a particular concern, and the DEA has taken or proposed separate scheduling actions involving elevated 7-OH and related substances," he told Fox News Digital. Vasquez said Mitra9’s products are made with botanical kratom extract derived from the natural leaf, and not with isolated or synthetic 7-OH. The products are labeled for adults 21 and older and include precautionary statements, he noted. The label advises consumers not to exceed the recommended serving, avoid use during pregnancy or breastfeeding, consult a physician before use if taking medications or managing a medical condition, avoid combining the product with alcohol or other substances, be aware that it may be habit-forming, and keep it out of the reach of children. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "We take every report of harm seriously, and we don't dismiss those concerns," Vasquez said, adding that the kratom market is "not uniform." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Products range from standardized, tested beverages to concentrated and synthetic 7-OH products that federal regulators are now moving to schedule," he said. "We support that action and stronger national standards for testing, labeling, potency limits and age restrictions." "Consumers deserve to know exactly what is in what they buy, and bad actors should be removed from the market."

articles.title: ‘Miracle on the Hudson’ hero Sully Sullenberger reveals Alzheimer’s warning signs he missed years ago
articles.summary: Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger and wife Lorrie revealed the subtle behavioral shifts noticed years before his Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
articles.body: Captain Chesley "Sully" Sullenberger, the former airline pilot celebrated worldwide for safely landing US Airways Flight 1549 on the Hudson River in 2009, is taking on a new mission to raise awareness about the early signs of Alzheimer’s disease. Sullenberger, who was diagnosed with the disease in August 2025, spoke on "Good Morning America" alongside his wife, Lorrie, to share their personal experience with the condition. The couple revealed several subtle shifts in routine and behavior that began surfacing several years before he received an official medical evaluation. 'MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON' HERO CAPTAIN 'SULLY' SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER'S DIAGNOSIS Reflecting on the timeline leading up to her husband's formal assessment, Lorrie Sullenberger noted that small adjustments in everyday life slowly pointed toward a bigger shift. "A lot of what I think people see in the news are late-stage Alzheimer's symptoms. And, so, in the very beginning, they are so subtle. And my advice to someone would be, it's what's unusual for your person," she shared, emphasizing how early symptoms often manifest gradually rather than abruptly. TV NEWS ANCHORMAN REVEALS HE HAS ALZHEIMER'S DURING FINAL NIGHT HELMING BROADCAST Public understanding of Alzheimer’s disease frequently focuses on these late-stage symptoms, such as pronounced memory loss, severe disorientation or difficulty managing basic daily routines. However, medical experts say early-stage cognitive decline can be much harder to spot. "One of the first things I noticed was that it was harder and harder to remember people’s names, even people we knew," Sullenberger said. "That’s still an issue. Just forgetting things that I normally wouldn’t. Or repeating myself, not realizing that I just said that an hour ago." Early indicators of Alzheimer's often present as mild cognitive impairment or subtle changes tailored to an individual’s normal baseline, according to health resources like the Cleveland Clinic. These can include misplacing everyday items, mild difficulty finding the right words during conversations, subtle changes in mood or executive function or taking slightly longer to complete familiar tasks. "I’ve gone through harder things than this before," Sullenberger said in the interview. The former pilot may be best known for successfully performing the "Miracle on the Hudson" in January 2009. After US Airways Flight 1549 suffered a dual engine failure after a bird strike shortly after taking off from New York's LaGuardia Airport, Sullenberger drew on decades of flight experience to glide the Airbus A320 onto the frigid Hudson River, where all 155 passengers and crew survived, according to the National Transportation Safety Board. articles.title: Swansea woman's migraines dismissed by GP as 'dramatic'
articles.summary: Lauren had to abandon her career in the NHS after being left "in agony" due to her migraines.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains details and references to suicide

When Lauren Evans told her doctor she was suicidal because of the "pure agony" of her chronic migraine, she was told she was being dramatic.

Lauren, 29, was seven when she got her first migraine and went on to have them regularly - by the time she was 24, they were happening every day.

"People need to understand that a migraine is a full body experience," she said.

Migraines are often misunderstood as "just a headache" despite being a neurological condition that can leave people unable to work, socialise or function in everyday life, according to a migraine expert.

The Welsh government said it was working to improve access to neurological services.

Lauren, from Swansea, said: "Although the 'headache' is in the head it can affect body temperature, digestive system, speech, light sensitivity, limb numbness, ability to walk and carry out a journey, brain fog, sleep, neck pain, mood swings, visual aura, sound sensitivity, cravings, vertigo.

"I would wake up daily either in pain or worried about when it would start."

She also spent a huge amount of time researching triggers and spent "hundreds on various things just to see if that would help" - from vitamins to chiropractors.

Lauren was training to become a biomedical scientist in the NHS but the lights and overstimulation of Singleton Hospital were so intense she had daily migraines.

She added that she often felt dismissed by colleagues who implied she was faking her condition but was lucky that her manager was supportive.

Some colleagues would accommodate her by turning off the lights, she said, but others said: "If you don't get your annual leave approved, you can just say you've got a migraine and you won't come in.

"That was so untrue. So you're battling, not just your physical health. You're battling all the mental side that comes with it as well.

"If I went home every day at the sight of a migraine, I would never be in work. There wasn't a day without pain and if there was, I'd be waiting for it."

To manage her symptoms, Lauren changed her working hours, starting at 08:00 BST and finishing at 16:00 so she could get home to take medication, but was still "in agony".

"I couldn't make plans because I knew I'd be suffering in the evening. My weekends would basically be spent recovering," she said.

Lauren said frequent attacks affected her relationship and left her feeling isolated: "It was a dark time. It got to the point where I was like, 'I can't do this for another year'."

Lauren said she went back to the doctor to try to find another option.

"I was like I've tried quite a lot of things. Is there any referrals I can have?

"I actually disclosed that I'm starting to feel suicidal and I'll never forget the words out of her mouth because I burst into tears immediately - she said: 'That sounds very dramatic, doesn't it?'

"I told her I had written a note to my family to say I couldn't live with the pain anymore."

She was referred to a neurologist, but four years on and she still has not been able to speak to them.

Lauren saw a crisis team in December, was signed off work for a month and her migraine attacks began to ease.

She decided it was time to leave her biomedical scientist career and now has a job at an insurance firm, and feels like a different person.

"I have never done so many hobbies in my life," she said.

"Jewellery making, painting... and running 50k in September for a charity."

Her new medication is working well, but she added: "If it got bad again, I honestly wouldn't know where to turn to."

Swansea Bay health board said it was "very sorry to hear of the patient's concerns" but could not comment on individual cases without consent and "would welcome the patient getting in touch with us so we can discuss this further".

It said it had a "specialist headache clinic that covers conditions such as migraine, which GPs can refer people to when appropriate".

Experiences like Lauren's are all too common, said Katy Munro, senior GP headache specialist at the National Migraine Centre and host of the Heads Up podcast.

"There are various barriers to people getting good help for migraine," she said.

"What we're trying to get away from is that preconception that migraine is just a very bad headache."

What is the difference between a migraine and a headache?

Munro said headaches were a symptom of migraine attacks, but so too are "visual disturbances, nausea and vomiting, sometimes numbness and tingling, sometimes abdominal pain, sometimes dizziness".

They are also a spectrum condition, she said, from episodic - meaning people have mild or rare attacks - to chronic where they have more than 15 days a month affected by migraine symptoms.

"If you have a migraine attack and you put up with it and then you have another one and put up with it, your brain actually gets more irritable," she said.

That means the migraines become more regular and can become chronic if effective treatment is not applied.

The first barrier to treatment, Munro said, is that a lot of people believe they are "normal headaches".

She said people should always get repetitive headaches checked out by a GP.

The next barrier is that GPs often just note down the headaches as a symptom rather than diagnose migraine.

The third barrier is the medication that was offered in the past, though this has improved in the last five years, she said.

"We need better education throughout the whole of society about how significant migraine is to people who suffer from it."

The Welsh government said it recognised the effect migraines can have on people's lives and that guidance was available to help NHS staff diagnose and manage conditions.

The UK government said National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had "clear guidance on the diagnosis and management of migraines, and we expect healthcare professionals to follow it and deliver high-quality care to all patients".

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line .

articles.title: CDC reports first measles death amid confusion over Pennsylvania cases
articles.summary: The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month.
articles.body: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention acknowledged Wednesday that one measles death has occurred so far in 2026 but provided no clarity about who died or where. The agency previously declined to recognize four measles-associated deaths the Pennsylvania Health Department reported over the last month. On Wednesday, the CDC’s measles outbreak page was updated to show one death with a note that the number “is subject to change” and that the agency will “update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” The change left more questions than answers. The CDC declined to provide details about which death it was referring to or whether it occurred in Pennsylvania. The agency said its National Center for Health Statistics had verified that the death now posted on the CDC website had occurred and that measles had been listed as an underlying cause of death. Two of the people whose deaths health officials reported in Pennsylvania were babies, including a newborn whose mother had measles while she was pregnant. One was a 40-year-old woman who had a history of asthma and severe lung disease, and another was an 18-year-old who developed a rare neurological condition that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. A Pennsylvania Health Department spokesperson said the department did not know which death the CDC was citing. Pennsylvania’s Health Department considers a death to be “measles associated” if the person died within 30 days of showing symptoms and testing positive for the virus. It can also take into account people’s medical records and whether they were exposed to measles before they died. The CDC’s website says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” As of Wednesday, the CDC had confirmed 3,471 measles cases in 45 states and Washington, D.C., this year. More than 300 people have been hospitalized because of measles infection. Three people died of measles in 2025: an adult in New Mexico and two young girls in Texas. The CDC readily acknowledged those deaths at the time based on information from state health departments. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania Health Department reported that its measles case count has soared to 835, with 111 cases in the last seven days. Two-thirds of those cases are in adults, and 164 people have been hospitalized in the state. Nearly all people who have been diagnosed with measles are unvaccinated. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are typically given around ages 1 and 5 and offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life. During measles outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old can receive booster doses.

articles.title: Over 160,000 pounds of meat recalled due to lack of inspection, labeled highest risk by USDA
articles.summary: Uninspected food “may contain undeclared allergens, harmful bacteria, or other contaminants that put consumer health and safety at risk,” the recall announcement said.
articles.body: Star Meat Delivery Inc. of Lucama, North Carolina, is recalling about 167,639 pounds of raw pork, beef and goat products, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture announcement posted Tuesday. The items were produced without the benefit of federal inspection, meaning they weren’t confirmed to be “safe, wholesome and properly labeled” by the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS). The recalled meat is also labeled with a false USDA mark of inspection, the announcement added. This recall has been classified as class I, the highest health risk. This classification refers to “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death,” according to the Food and Drug Administration. Which products are being recalled? Any meat product produced by Star Meat Delivery Inc. with an inspection and establishment number that reads “EST. 1363” is falsely labeled, according to the announcement. Consider it misbranded and unsafe to eat, the FSIS warned. The vacuum-sealed raw pork, beef and goat products were produced on various dates before Sept. 22, 2026. They were packed into cardboard boxes ahead of shipping, and once they arrived at their destinations, may have been relabeled with the respective retailer’s sticker and handling instructions, the announcement said. The FSIS will update the product list as it gathers more information, but as of Wednesday, the following products with the A&D Foods label are subject to recall: Various weight cardboard boxes articles.title: Just one small serving of ultra-processed food a day linked to higher disease risk, major study finds
articles.summary: A study of nearly 8.8 million adults links every extra 100 grams of ultra-processed foods daily to higher risks of cardiovascular disease and cancer.
articles.body: Just an extra 3½ ounces of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) a day was linked to a higher risk of chronic disease, according to a new large-scale analysis. The study, published Sept. 22 in the journal Family Medicine and Community Health, looked at nearly 8.8 million adults who participated in studies across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Oceania, with follow-up periods ranging from two to 32 years. For every additional 100 grams of UPFs consumed daily, researchers found an association with a 14% higher risk of cardiovascular events, a 4% higher risk of cancer, a 3% higher risk of death from any cause and a 2% higher risk of metabolic syndrome or diabetes, according to a news release. BRINGING THIS POPULAR DRINK TO A JOB INTERVIEW COULD HURT YOUR CHANCES, EXPERTS WARN UPFs are typically packaged and convenient, made through extensive industrial processing and often packed with additives. They can include sugary drinks, processed meats, packaged snacks and candy. One hundred grams is about the size of a 3½-ounce bag of corn chips, a small box of candy or a single-serve cup of mini cookies. People with the highest intake of UPFs also had higher risks of digestive diseases, depression or anxiety, obesity, cancer and cardiovascular events than those with the lowest intake of the foods. 5 ULTRA-PROCESSED FOODS THAT MAY BE WORSE FOR YOUR HEALTH THAN YOU THINK, EXPERT SAYS "Given that UPF-related chronic diseases often cluster as multimorbidity, reducing consumption of UPFs and replacing them with minimally processed alternatives may be relevant for chronic disease prevention and primary care management," wrote the researchers, led by Xiao Liu, a cardiologist at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital in China and a research fellow at Duke-NUS Medical School in Singapore. "A diet built around whole, minimally processed foods is one of the best investments we can make in our long-term health." These types of foods tend to crowd out healthier, nutrient-dense options, according to Kelly Springer, a New York-based registered dietitian and founder of Kelly's Choice. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It's not that you can never eat them again," Springer, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital. "It's the fact that we are not getting real foods — real foods like fruits, vegetables, beans, nuts, whole grains." Rather than focusing on taking foods away, Springer recommended adding protein and fiber to meals and snacks. She suggested options such as an apple with peanut butter, nuts with cucumbers or meals built around beans, chicken or tuna alongside fruits, vegetables and whole grains. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "A diet built around whole, minimally processed foods is one of the best investments we can make in our long-term health," she added. Springer noted that the study was observational, so it cannot establish that UPFs directly caused the poor health outcomes. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER It also relied on participants' self-reported diets and may not be able to account for other lifestyle factors. Nonetheless, the study can teach people about the link between ultra-processed foods and chronic disease, Springer said. articles.title: Centro Médico Pastore oferece exames e consultas especializadas em Petrópolis | G1
articles.standfirst: Unidade na Praça dos Expedicionários conta com exames laboratoriais e de imagem, além de consultas em mais de 40 especialidades médicas.
articles.summary: Unidade na Praça dos Expedicionários conta com exames laboratoriais e de imagem, além de consultas em mais de 40 especialidades médicas.
articles.body:
Centro Médico Pastore Unidade Petrópolis — Foto: Arquivo interno

De análises laboratoriais a exames de imagem e avaliações cardiológicas, o Centro Médico Pastore reúne em Petrópolis procedimentos para diferentes necessidades de saúde. A unidade fica na Praça dos Expedicionários, no Centro, e atende tanto a pedidos de exames de rotina quanto a investigações mais específicas.

Centro Médico Pastore Unidade, Praça dos Expedicionários — Foto: Arquivo interno

Entre as opções estão raios X, mamografia e ultrassonografia, além de endoscopia digestiva alta, na área de Gastroenterologia. A relação inclui também ecodoppler e exames voltados à avaliação cardiovascular, como eletrocardiograma, Holter e MAPA 24h. Esses são alguns dos procedimentos disponíveis. A relação completa pode ser consultada pelo site, pela Central de Atendimento ou diretamente na unidade de Petrópolis.

O paciente também encontra consultas em mais de 40 especialidades médicas, entre elas Clínica Geral, Cardiologia, Ginecologia, Ortopedia e Gastroenterologia.

De acordo com a disponibilidade da agenda, da indicação médica e do preparo necessário, a consulta e os exames podem ser realizados no mesmo dia, trazendo mais praticidade e agilidade ao paciente ao concentrar diferentes etapas do atendimento em um só lugar.

Centro Médico Pastore Unidade, Exames laboratoriais e de imagem — Foto: Arquivo interno

Os agendamentos podem ser feitos pelo site ou pela Central de Atendimento, que fornece informações sobre os procedimentos e as orientações de preparo.

articles.title: Jovem com paralisia cerebral consegue vaga em enfermaria no DF | G1
articles.standfirst: Weverton Alan Alves Garcia, de 21 anos, aguardava uma vaga em quarto desde que recebeu alta da terapia intensiva. Nesta quarta-feira (23), ele foi transferido para um leito no Hospital Regional de Samambaia.
articles.summary: Weverton Garcia, de 21 anos, foi transferido para o Hospital Regional de Samambaia após aguardar 10 dias por um leito de enfermaria mesmo com alta médica da UTI.
articles.body:
Na terça (22), o g1 mostrou a história de Weverton Alan Alves Garcia , de 21 anos.

A família informou que, nesta quarta, o jovem conseguiu a tão esperada vaga. O jovem usa traqueostomia e recebe alimentação por gastrostomia (GTT).

"Depois de tantos dias de espera e preocupação, essa foi uma vitória enorme para toda a nossa família", disse Tainá Garcia, irmã de Weverton.

➡️ Na terça, a Secretaria de Saúde do Distrito Federal havia confirmado ao g1 que não havia vaga de enfermaria de clínica médica disponível para o paciente – nem no Hospital Regional de Samambaia , nem no Hospital Regional do Paranoá, unidade indicada como referência para a região onde ele mora.

Relatório médico mostra que a alta ocorreu em 13 de setembro. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A alta da UTI havia sido registrada em relatório médico de 13 de setembro . O documento informava que Weverton estava em regular estado geral, respirava espontaneamente pela traqueostomia, sem desconforto ou queda de saturação, e estava sem febre.

Weverton havia sido transferido da UPA de São Sebastião para a UTI do Hospital Regional de Samambaia em 31 de agosto, após apresentar pneumonia complicada por derrame pleural e evoluir para choque séptico de origem pulmonar.
